analysis.one_liner: Restricts tobacco ads near schools and in youth media while barring FDA tobacco regulation.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote, and died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned tobacco billboards within 500 feet of schools, tobacco ads in publications whose readers are more than 15 percent under 18, and paid product placement in movies and video games. It also would have conditioned federal substance-abuse grants on states banning tobacco sales to minors, unsupervised vending machines, and free samples. Its final provision went the other way: it would have permanently barred the Food and Drug Administration from regulating tobacco in any manner.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teens would have seen less tobacco advertising near schools, in youth-oriented magazines, and in movies and games. States would have kept federal substance-abuse grant money by passing youth-access laws and could have used that money to enforce bans on selling tobacco to minors and on free samples.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and teens exposed to tobacco marketing

how_it_helps.text: Would have made it unlawful to advertise cigarettes or smokeless tobacco on billboards within 500 feet of any elementary or secondary school.
Would have banned tobacco ads in newspapers and magazines whose under-18 readers make up more than 15 percent of the audience, with the FTC publishing an annual list of affected publications.

Would have prohibited manufacturers from paying to place cigarettes or smokeless tobacco as props in movies, and barred brand names and logos in videos, on video game machines, and at family amusement centers.

Starting in fiscal 1997, states would have qualified for federal substance-abuse block grants only if they banned tobacco sales to anyone under 18, required vending machines to be under direct supervision, and prohibited free distribution of tobacco and coupon redemption, with grant money usable to enforce those laws.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers would have lost advertising channels; billboard owners and youth-oriented publications would have lost tobacco ad revenue; movie studios and game or amusement operators would have lost paid-placement income; retailers and vending operators would have faced new limits on sales, samples, and coupons; and states would have had to enact and enforce the specified laws or risk losing federal substance-abuse grant money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco firms, billboard owners, and publishers

drawbacks.text: The final section would have declared that nothing in any law gives the FDA any authority to regulate tobacco in any manner, permanently foreclosing federal oversight of nicotine content, additives, and marketing beyond whatever Congress itself chose to write.

With the FDA barred, the bill's advertising limits would have become a statutory ceiling rather than a floor, leaving Congress as the only route to tighter rules, in a body where the bill drew no cosponsors.

The restrictions carried broad exceptions: billboards beside interstates aimed away from schools, street-level signs at stores selling tobacco, and coupons distributed by mail, in unrestricted publications, or to adults with photo ID would all have remained legal.
States that did not meet the new conditions on youth-access laws would have risked losing federal substance-abuse prevention and treatment grants, reducing their flexibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The marketing limits and enforcement money would have made tobacco harder for children to see and buy, and that had real value. But the price was Section 5's total ban on FDA authority over tobacco, taken while the FDA was moving to assert exactly that authority over cigarettes and smokeless products. A modest set of advertising limits, with wide exceptions, traded for a permanent shield against the strongest federal regulator of a product that is the leading preventable cause of death is a trade whose weight falls on the industry's side. The bill's structure helps explain why it drew no cosponsors from either party.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Wendell Ford of Kentucky introduced the Tobacco Products Control Act of 1995 on September 20, 1995, and delivered introductory remarks the same day.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on September 20, 1995.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor; the bill's cosponsor count stayed at zero.
The Commerce Committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote. The bill's action history ends with the referral, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, killing the bill.

The bill was introduced while the FDA was in the process of asserting jurisdiction over tobacco, and the measure's last section would have stripped that authority by statute; that provision never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody got what they wanted from this bill: tobacco companies did not win their statutory exemption from FDA regulation, and the advertising limits never took effect either. Public health came out ahead on the provision that mattered most, because the permanent ban on FDA tobacco regulation never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco got no FDA exemption; regulators stayed free

for.name: Sen. Wendell Ford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor; served as its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 20, 1995, and never held a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Larry Pressler
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman during the 104th Congress, took no action to schedule the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill's partisan shape cannot be measured; a lone Democrat introduced it into a Republican-led Senate and it died without either party acting.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed modest new limits on how tobacco is advertised while writing into law that no agency, ever, could regulate tobacco, locking in the industry's freedom from FDA oversight of nicotine, ingredients, and marketing. The shield is worth far more than the ad limits it costs, which is why the trade favors the industry even though the bill carries restrictions.

Billboard operators would have lost tobacco accounts within 500 feet of schools, with exceptions for interstate-facing and street-level retail signs. The revenue loss is modest but the restriction would have removed large tobacco signs from children's daily routes.

Publications whose readership is more than 15 percent under 18 would have lost tobacco advertising, a category the FTC would have listed annually. Tobacco ads are lucrative, so this would have cut revenue for youth-oriented titles.

industries.industry: Movie studios and video game or amusement operators
industries.note: The bill would have banned paid tobacco product placement in movies and brand logos in videos, on game machines, and at family amusement centers, ending placement fees. This closes a channel that puts brands in front of children.

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers and vending machine operators
industries.note: States keeping their grants would have had to require vending machines to be under direct adult supervision and to ban free samples and coupon redemption, limiting unsupervised sales channels. Some machine and sample exceptions for bars, private clubs, and adult-only locations would have remained.
